documents.unit: AI at CWRU (AI Governance Committee, AI Task Force)
documents.title: Governance & Policies | AI at CWRU
documents.stance_why: The page sets university-wide principles but no AI stance for coursework: it requires integrity and approved tools, and says "Faculty retain discretion over whether and how to incorporate AI", so it delegates.
documents.summary: CWRU's university AI governance page. It binds all users to existing integrity, acceptable-use and data policies, requires approved tools and bars restricted data from AI, and leaves classroom AI decisions to faculty. Also describes the governance bodies.

units.why: The opening sentence states the institution-wide principle ("supports the responsible and innovative use of AI"), so it is a framework preamble (P56) rather than a rule for a specific actor; it welcomes AI, hence permit.
units.anchor: CWRU supports the responsible and innovative use of AI

units.why: "including generative and agentic AI systems" sets what kind of AI the policy covers, a scope definition (P61), not a rule.
units.anchor: including generative and agentic AI systems

units.why: "Rather than establishing AI policies in isolation... builds upon existing institutional requirements" states the framework principle that AI is governed through existing integrity, security and privacy policies; P56 fits, no stance taken.
units.anchor: Rather than establishing AI policies in isolation
units.frag_start: Rather than establishing AI policies in

units.why: "must use AI with integrity, transparency and accountability in accordance with applicable university policies" binds everyone and conditions AI use on existing policies; this is the general framework rule (P56), AI is permitted with conditions.
units.anchor: must use AI with integrity, transparency and accountability
units.frag_start: All members of the university community

units.why: "Users remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity and appropriate use of AI-assisted work" makes users answerable for what they produce with AI, so P29 fits better than P31 because it is about responsibility, not only verification.
units.anchor: Users remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity and appropriate use of AI-assisted work.

units.why: "Faculty retain discretion over whether and how to incorporate AI" leaves the decision to individual faculty, which is P04; it sets no stance itself.
units.anchor: Faculty retain discretion over whether and how to incorporate AI

units.why: "Use university-approved AI tools" directs users to vetted tools for university work; P50 (prefer vetted tools) fits rather than P17 because the university does not here supply a specific course tool.
units.anchor: Use university-approved AI tools.

units.why: "Avoid personal or unapproved consumer AI accounts, which may not provide the same data privacy and security protections" discourages unvetted tools for data-protection reasons (P50); "Avoid" is should-not.
units.anchor: Avoid personal or unapproved consumer AI accounts

units.why: "Do not enter restricted university data... into any AI tool" is a flat ban on entering sensitive data, a data-protection rule (P50), not about assignments (so not P20).
units.anchor: Do not enter restricted university data

units.why: "Review applicable data security guidelines and research requirements before uploading documents" asks users to check data rules first; P50 data protection, imperative so should.
units.anchor: Review applicable data security guidelines and research requirements before uploading documents

units.why: The governance structure (AI Governance Committee, AI Strategy Committee, AI Task Force, working groups) says who oversees AI institutionally; it is a framework/oversight fact (P56) with no rule for use.
units.anchor: the AI Governance Committee and the AI Strategy Committee provide strategic direction and institutional oversight

units.why: "Use this form to report potential risks or inappropriate AI use" gives a reporting channel for AI concerns; it is enforcement-related but no type covers reporting channels (P36 is classification as misconduct, P64 is student response).
units.anchor: Use this form to report potential risks or inappropriate AI use.
units.uncovered_note: A reporting channel (form) for AI security, privacy or misuse concerns.

documents.title: Guidance on integrating AI (artificial intelligence) into the CWRU classroom
documents.stance_why: The provost letter says "Faculty members have complete discretion" and lists a range from prohibition to open use with citation, so no single stance is set; it delegates.
documents.summary: A 2023 provost letter giving faculty full discretion over student AI use, asking them to state expectations in every syllabus and enforce integrity standards, and noting AI-detection tools may be used. Announces a faculty committee on AI in teaching.

units.why: The provost says students who "use unapproved AI tools may be shortcutting the learning process to their ultimate disadvantage", a rationale that AI bypasses the practice that builds skill (P41); informs.
units.anchor: students who use unapproved AI tools may be shortcutting the learning process

units.why: "it is important for us to explore and to adapt to new technologies to better serve our students, since they will likely live in an increasingly technological world" justifies AI engagement by future needs (P44).
units.anchor: it is important for us to explore and to adapt to new technologies
units.frag_start: it is important for us to

units.why: "Faculty members have complete discretion regarding the extent to which they will allow AI tools" hands the decision to each instructor, P04, with no university default.
units.anchor: Faculty members have complete discretion regarding the extent to which they will allow AI tools

units.why: The list "(a) completely prohibiting... (b) asking that students consult with instructors for permission... (c) allowing students to use all AI tools" names a spectrum of options, so P05 (named levels) fits better than P04, which is about who decides.
units.anchor: completely prohibiting the use of AI tools

units.why: Option (c) expects that "students will properly cite their usage of such tools", a citation/disclosure expectation (P24) attached to open use.
units.anchor: students will properly cite their usage of such tools

units.why: "Faculty should clearly communicate expectations regarding the use of AI tools to students in all course syllabi" is a syllabus-statement requirement (P09) addressed to faculty.
units.anchor: Faculty should clearly communicate expectations regarding the use of AI tools

units.why: "Faculty must enforce high ethical standards for students' academic conduct" requires instructors to enforce integrity rules; P36 (handled through integrity processes) is the closest.
units.anchor: Faculty must enforce high ethical standards for students’ academic conduct.

units.why: "The university's various Academic Integrity policies prohibit academic dishonesty, including misrepresentation of a student's own work" says students' submissions must be their own (P29); AI is not named but the paragraph frames AI conduct.
units.anchor: prohibit academic dishonesty, including misrepresentation of a student’s own work

units.why: "Faculty may take advantage of software tools that can detect the use of AI by students" permits detector use, P40 (tools used to identify misuse), not P39 as it does not say detectors are unreliable.
units.anchor: Faculty may take advantage of software tools that can detect the use of AI

units.why: The provost is "working with the Faculty Senate to form a committee to explore the broader implications of AI on teaching", a commitment to keep studying and revisiting AI policy (P54).
units.anchor: form a committee to explore the broader implications of AI on teaching

documents.unit: Office of the Provost (AI Task Force)
documents.title: Example AI Policies, Suitable for Course Syllabi
documents.stance_why: The page offers four sample syllabus texts from "No AI Usage Allowed" to "Unrestricted AI Usage" as "a starting point", so it is a set of tiers for instructors to choose from; it delegates.
tiers: Restricted AI Usage for Specific Tasks
documents.summary: Provost AI Task Force sample syllabus statements in four tiers, from a full ban to unrestricted use, framed as templates that respect faculty academic freedom.

units.why: "embraces AI in education to prepare students for the workforce" gives a career rationale for AI (P44) and signals encouragement at the university level.
units.anchor: embraces AI in education to prepare students for the workforce
units.frag_start: Case Western Reserve University embraces AI

units.why: "the university respects faculty's academic freedom to manage their classes" leaves AI rules to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: respects faculty's academic freedom to manage their classes

units.why: The page presents four sample syllabus texts ranging from "No AI Usage Allowed" to "Unrestricted AI Usage", i.e. named levels of AI use (P05), offered as "a starting point", not mandated.
units.anchor: This list of sample texts serves as a starting point for syllabi
units.frag_end: how AI tools might be used.

units.why: Template 1 states "Students are prohibited from using any AI tools... for any aspect of the course", a default ban on all course work (P01).
units.anchor: Students are prohibited from using any AI tools, algorithms, or technologies

units.why: "any violation of this policy may result in academic penalties" states consequences only vaguely; P37 (penalties in advance) is the closest type, though no specific penalty is named.
units.anchor: any violation of this policy may result in academic penalties

units.why: "Students are encouraged to consult with the instructor if they have any questions or concerns regarding the appropriate use of common/basic AI" tells students to ask when unsure (P10). The same sentence recurs in templates 2-4 and is coded once.
units.anchor: encouraged to consult with the instructor if they have any questions or concerns
units.frag_end: use of common/basic AI in this course.

units.why: Template 2 says "Students are expected to use AI responsibly and critically evaluate the outputs of AI tools", requiring evaluation of output (P31); the sentence recurs in templates 3 and 4 and is coded once.
units.anchor: critically evaluate the outputs of AI tools

units.why: "Students can use basic AI tools for specific tasks approved by the instructor, such as grammar checking or citation formatting" allows only narrow listed uses; grammar/citation tasks make this P18 (prose tools) rather than P16.
units.anchor: Students can use basic AI tools for specific tasks approved by the instructor

units.why: "students must demonstrate a clear understanding of both the AI methods employed and their academic application" requires understanding of what is used (P30).
units.anchor: students must demonstrate a clear understanding of both the AI methods employed
units.frag_start: The use of AI should be

units.why: Template 3: "AI tools and methodologies are encouraged to enhance learning outcomes" sets an encouraging default (P02).
units.anchor: AI tools and methodologies are encouraged to enhance learning outcomes

units.why: "Guidelines for AI usage will be provided to ensure alignment with course objectives and academic standards" commits the instructor to communicate expectations (P09).
units.anchor: Guidelines for AI usage will be provided

units.why: Template 4: "Students have full autonomy to utilize AI technologies for all aspects of the course, including assignments, projects, research, and examinations" freely permits AI, even on exams (P02).
units.anchor: Students have full autonomy to utilize AI technologies for all aspects of the course

documents.unit: University Center for Innovation in Teaching and Education (UCITE)
documents.title: Teaching and Learning with Generative Artificial Intelligence Systems
documents.stance_why: The teaching center page advises faculty how to set and communicate their own policies ("Create, or co-create with students, appropriate policies") and sets no student rule of its own; it delegates.
documents.summary: UCITE advice for faculty on teaching with GenAI: learn the tools, talk openly with students, set or co-create course policies, point to integrity policies, and protect sensitive data. Links a living survey of faculty syllabus statements.

units.why: UCITE says faculty "can and should take time to reflect how, when, and where we improve student learning" with GenAI before deciding, i.e. faculty learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: faculty can and should take time to reflect how, when, and where

units.why: "UCITE can work with faculty to consider how course learning objectives or goals align with student assessments" offers consultation support (P63).
units.anchor: UCITE can work with faculty to consider how course learning objectives

units.why: The Canvas course "Getting Started with Generative AI in Education" is faculty training (P63).
units.anchor: launched a Canvas course for faculty and staff members titled

units.why: "Take some time to experience and experiment with GenAI tools" advises faculty to try tools before setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: Take some time to experience and experiment with GenAI tools
units.frag_end: CWRU AI, Microsoft CoPilot, and ChatGPT.

units.why: "Never put sensitive university information into an AI service if the university does not have a contract" is a data-protection rule preferring vetted tools (P50).
units.anchor: Never put sensitive university information into an AI service

units.why: "have open and transparent conversations with students about your expectations regarding ChatGPT or other GenAI tools" tells instructors to communicate expectations (P09).
units.anchor: have open and transparent conversations with students about your expectations
units.frag_end: use of those systems in our courses.

units.why: "try not to rush to an assumption that students are necessarily going to cheat using GenAI tools" asks instructors to presume good faith; no type covers this stance, P57 is about talking before escalation.
units.anchor: try not to rush to an assumption that students are necessarily going to cheat
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should not presume that students will cheat with GenAI (presumption of good faith).

units.why: "Create, or co-create with students, appropriate policies for ChatGPT use" has instructors set their own course policy, with student input (P04).
units.anchor: Create, or co-create with students, appropriate policies for ChatGPT use

units.why: "ensure that students understand the policies and the consequences for not adhering" is about making expectations clear to students (P09); consequences are not specified so not P37.
units.anchor: ensure that students understand the policies and the consequences for not adhering

units.why: "Remind students of CWRU Policies related to appropriate use of AI tools, including CWRU Academic Integrity policies" ties AI misuse to the integrity policy (P36).
units.anchor: CWRU Academic Integrity policies
units.frag_end: relevant to student use of AI tools in your course.

units.why: "Consider a discussion about the ethical choices around accessing, using, and contributing to GenAI tools" recommends raising ethics with students (P53).
units.anchor: Consider a discussion about the ethical choices around accessing, using, and contributing

units.why: The resource list item "AI Detection Services: Use with Caution" advises caution with detectors; P39 is the closest type though it does not say they are unreliable.
units.anchor: AI Detection Services: Use with Caution

units.why: The "living" survey of faculty syllabus statements "will change as updates are submitted", a maintained resource for syllabus language (P63) with an ongoing-revision element.
units.anchor: This is a “living” document and will change as updates are submitted.
units.frag_start: Teaching faculty were asked to share

notes: Coder B. No computing, school or course documents were collected. Repeated template sentences in the example-policies page are coded once.
